title: The Reweighting Principle in Statistical Mechanics
abstract: Reweighting of probability measures provides a unifying perspective on conditioning, exponential tilting, and, more generally, ensemble transformations in statistical mechanics. We show that exponential tilting and conditioning arise as the minimum-relative-entropy updates associated with soft and hard constraints, respectively. Their relative entropies naturally inherit complementary thermodynamic structures: exponential tilting gives rise to the Legendre structure of the canonical ensemble and reduces to the Gibbs entropy for a uniform reference measure, while conditioning reduces to the Boltzmann entropy through the surprisal of the constrained macrostate. By introducing an enlarged probability space in which observables are treated as explicit variables, we further show that microcanonical and canonical ensembles arise as conditional and marginal distributions of a common structural prior after exponential reweighting. In the thermodynamic limit, described through large deviation theory, conditioning emerges from exponential tilting by concentration of measure, revealing ensemble equivalence as a consequence of entropy--bias competition. Finally, we outline how the same information-theoretic framework naturally extends to path space, suggesting a unified probabilistic description of equilibrium thermodynamics and conditioned stochastic dynamics.
summary: The paper unifies statistical mechanics by showing that both soft constraints (exponential tilting, leading to the canonical ensemble) and hard constraints (conditioning, leading to the microcanonical ensemble) are mathematically equivalent formulations derived from minimizing relative entropy. By enlarging the state space, it provides a single information-theoretic lens through which equilibrium thermodynamics can be understood.
main_problem: To develop a unified probabilistic framework connecting conditioning, exponential tilting, and ensemble transformations within statistical mechanics.
main_result: The paper shows that both canonical (soft constraint) and microcanonical (hard constraint) ensembles arise naturally as minimum relative entropy updates from a common structural prior. In the thermodynamic limit, these distinct descriptions become macroscopically equivalent.
method: It employs information theory, specifically minimizing the Kullback–Leibler divergence (relative entropy), applied to an enlarged probability space where observables are explicit variables.
model_or_system: The system is general statistical ensembles ($ho$), modeled by constraining a reference measure $ho_0$ via soft constraints (exponential tilting) or hard constraints (conditioning).
key_observables: Gibbs entropy, Boltzmann entropy, Relative Entropy, Free-energy potential, and the observable $A(x)$.
important_parameters: The tilting parameter ($\lambda$), the fixed constraint value ($ ar{A}$), and the thermodynamic limit ($N 	o \infty$).
main_assumptions: Conditioning is treated as a formal limit rather than a standard measure change, and ensemble equivalence is established only in the macroscopic (thermodynamic) limit.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates the smooth reshaping (orange) versus support restriction (green) of the reference ensemble; Table 1 summarizes soft vs. hard constraints and resulting ensembles.
paper_structure: The paper builds from defining reweighting principles, deriving both exponential tilting (canonical/Gibbs structure) and conditioning (microcanonical/Boltzmann structure) via minimum relative entropy, unifying them through an enlarged space construction, and finally demonstrating their macroscopic equivalence in the thermodynamic limit.
why_interesting: This work provides a deep information-theoretic underpinning for fundamental concepts like ensemble equivalence, which is crucial when modeling quantum systems where different approximations (e.g., mean-field vs. exact) might be used.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Schematic illustration of soft and hard reweighting. Exponential tilting (orange) modifies the reference ensemble (blue) smoothly through an exponential weight, while conditioning (green) selects a finite-resolution macrostate associated with a prescribed value of the observable. These two operations provide the probabilistic prototype for canonical and microcanonical constructions, respectively.
